passages.text: SCARLET FEVER, or SCARLATINA, a fever attended with a red eruption, which spreads over the whole skin in large patches, and makes it appear as if it were dyed with scarlet.
The disease is commonly joined with a soreness of the throat and a difficulty of swallowing; and it attacks children more frequently than grown persons.
It is ascribed by physicians to an acrid humour in the blood, which nature throws out upon the skin; others derive it from a putrid state of the air.
In its common form it is a mild disease, and seldom proves fatal, if the patient be kept from cold and from hot medicines.
The malignant kind, with an ulcerated throat, is contagious, and has sometimes swept away the children of whole families.
The cure consists in bleeding, if the fever run high, in gentle purges, and in a cooling diet; the patient is to drink plentifully of barley-water and lemonade.
When the redness goes off, the scarf-skin falls off in scales, and sometimes the skin of the hands peels away entire like a glove.
Scarlet fever, also known as scarlatina, is an infectious disease caused by Streptococcus pyogenes, a group A streptococcus. It most commonly affects children between five and fifteen years of age.
Signs and symptoms include a sore throat, fever, headache, swollen lymph nodes and a typical rash. The rash is red and feels like sandpaper, and the tongue may be red and bumpy.
The disease is caused by strains of group A streptococcus that release toxins. It spreads mainly through respiratory droplets when an infected person coughs or sneezes.
In the 19th century scarlet fever was a major cause of death in children in Europe and North America, with large epidemics.
Treatment with antibiotics such as penicillin shortens the illness and prevents complications such as rheumatic fever. With treatment, deaths are rare.
As the rash fades after about a week, the skin may peel, especially on the hands and feet.
There is no vaccine against scarlet fever. Prevention depends on hand washing and on keeping sick people away from others.

reasons: Same name: SCARLET FEVER, or SCARLATINA, and Scarlet fever, also known as scarlatina.
Both texts describe the red rash, the sore throat and the peeling skin.
Streptococcal pharyngitis scores well but covers the throat infection without the rash.

alignments.label: Red rash

britannica.quote: a red eruption, which spreads over the whole skin

wikipedia.quote: The rash is red and feels like sandpaper

alignments.note: Same sign. Change in language only.

alignments.label: Sore throat
alignments.note: Same fact, almost the same words.

alignments.label: Mostly children

britannica.quote: it attacks children more frequently than grown persons

alignments.note: Both say the disease mostly strikes children.

alignments.label: Cause

britannica.quote: an acrid humour in the blood

alignments.note: Change in knowledge. A bacterium causes the disease, not a humour or putrid air.

alignments.label: Contagion

britannica.quote: The malignant kind, with an ulcerated throat, is contagious

wikipedia.quote: It spreads mainly through respiratory droplets

alignments.note: The 1797 text calls only the malignant kind contagious. Today all forms are known to spread from person to person.

alignments.label: A mild disease

britannica.quote: In its common form it is a mild disease, and seldom proves fatal

wikipedia.quote: a major cause of death in children

alignments.note: Mild cases occur, but in the 19th century the disease killed many children. Inference: the 1797 view reflects a period of milder outbreaks.

alignments.label: Cure

wikipedia.quote: Treatment with antibiotics such as penicillin

alignments.note: Change in knowledge. Bleeding does not treat the infection. Antibiotics do.

alignments.label: Peeling skin

britannica.quote: the scarf-skin falls off in scales

wikipedia.quote: the skin may peel, especially on the hands and feet

alignments.note: Same sign. The scarf-skin is the outer layer of the skin.

alignments.label: No vaccine

wikipedia.quote: There is no vaccine against scarlet fever

alignments.note: Wikipedia adds prevention. The 1797 text gives no advice on it.

suggestedQuestions: What did the 1797 entry say causes scarlet fever?
Was scarlet fever a mild disease?

What did the 1797 entry say causes scarl.answer: It names an acrid humour in the blood that nature throws out on the skin, or a putrid state of the air [B3]. Wikipedia names a bacterium, Streptococcus pyogenes [W1], whose strains release toxins and spread by droplets [W3].

Was scarlet fever a mild disease?.answer: The 1797 entry calls the common form mild and seldom fatal [B4], though it says the malignant kind could kill the children of whole families [B5]. Wikipedia says that in the 19th century it was a major cause of death in children [W4]. Today antibiotics make deaths rare [W5].
